There is a high-falling tone harmony process with a single word shown in (7) where the second syllable is originally with a mid-level-tone /ɲe²/. ... Shecyü has no stress. The author has observed occasional idiolectal tonal free-variation for some speakers in Chamchang, a Shecyü dialect found in India.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Shecyü (a Pangwa Tangsa variety) is a three-tone language (high-falling, mid-level, mid-falling on unchecked syllables; checked syllables non-contrastive) and the author states flatly that it has no stress. Word prosody is carried by tone; sesquisyllabic words have a toneless minor (schwa) syllable followed by a tone-bearing major syllable. Morey 2014 (LD&C 8: 661-662, Mueshaungx and Chamchang) adds the phonetic side: these languages are iambic, the first syllable of a disyllable is 'reduced and less stressed' (shorter, less intensity, reduced pitch fall), the second syllable is the prominent one.
new_statements.exceptions: None for stress. Tone: minor syllables of sesquisyllables are toneless (always mid pitch); syllabic nasal /m̩/ can carry contrastive tone; a high-tone harmony process within words (p. 44); Mungre likewise has toneless minor syllables (p. 65) but no stress statement is made for Mungre.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, based on elicited wordlist/citation forms (about 2,400 items per variety) plus recordings; Morey 2014's iambic/reduced-first-syllable observation concerns disyllabic words in citation form (kufkuf 'dog', wushawx 'bird').
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog 5.1 tase1235 covers the Pangwa Tangsa dialects (Cholim tong1312, Muishaung mosa1240, Mungre mung1264, Chamchang kims1240, Shecyu-Chamchang shec1234, Rera-Hajang rera1241, Joglei, Ngaimong, Hahcheng, Longri, Lochhang, Maitai, etc.). The quoted statement is about Shecyü (Myanmar; Chamchang is its Indian dialect) = shec1234/kims1240 under tase1235; Khan 2017 also covers Mungre (mung1264). The two sources the earlier scan named are OUTSIDE tase1235 in Glottolog: Boro 2017 Hakhun = hakh1236 (under Nocte Naga noct1238) and Mulder 2020 Muklom = mukl1235 (Muklomic mukl1234). Morey 2014 pp. 661-662 (Mueshaungx = mosa1240, Chamchang = kims1240) supports the reading for other Pangwa varieties.

sources.note: §3.2.2 Stress, pp. 71-72: sesquisyllabic words are minor-major, 'so the language falls under the group of languages which show iambic stress'; minor syllables toneless and unstressed; phonological word not yet established (p. ~160). Muklom is mukl1235 (Muklomic), not tase1235.

sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request); access check: online with a university library login
sources.note: §2.5 Stress, p. 63: 'Stress is not contrastive in Hakhun, most probably because one of the correlates of stress, namely pitch, is used for lexical contrast. In terms of enunciation, all syllables in multi-syllabic words are more or less equally enunciated.' Hakhun is hakh1236 (under Nocte Naga in Glottolog), not tase1235 — the scan's named source was misattributed.

sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: p. 661: 'the iambic nature of these languages makes the tonal profile of the first syllable less prominent' (Mueshaungx orthography leaves the first-syllable tone unmarked); p. 662, Chamchang kufkuf 'dog': first syllable shorter, less intensity, less pitch fall — 'My preferred analysis, however, is to treat the first syllable as reduced and less stressed one'. Three tones per variety (Cholim, Chamchang, Mueshaungx, etc.).
